name: Picts
info: The Picts were a group of peoples in what is now Scotland north of the Firth of Forth in the Early Middle Ages, remembered for their carved symbol stones, their silverwork and the kingdom of Fortriu.

facts.homeland: Scotland north of the Firth of Forth and the Forth-Clyde isthmus, outside Dál Riata in the west; the core of Fortriu lay around Moray and Inverness; sites include Burghead Fort, Portmahomack, Abernethy, Rosemarkie and Dunkeld
facts.period: the name Picti from the late third century AD (first in a panegyric of 297); several chiefdoms, then the Verturian hegemony of Fortriu from the seventh century, lasting about 160 years; merger with Dál Riata into the Kingdom of Alba in the ninth century; Pictish identity forgotten, probably by the 11th century
facts.known: Pictish symbol stones and cross-slabs; the Pictish Beast and the mirror and comb, double-disc and Z-rod and crescent and V-rod symbols; heavy silver chains; penannular brooches and the St Ninian's Isle Treasure; the Battle of Dun Nechtain in 685; an Insular Celtic language now extinct
facts.sources: outside writers: Roman panegyrics and Claudian, Bede's Ecclesiastical History, Adomnán's life of Columba, the Irish annals and the Pictish Chronicle; the stones and their inscriptions in Latin and ogham; excavations such as Martin Carver's at Portmahomack; a 2023 study of eight whole genomes from Lundin Links and Balintore

t: The name Picti appears in Roman sources from the end of the third century AD as an outsiders' term for unromanised people in northern Britain, and was most likely pejorative.
From the seventh century the kingdom of Fortriu, centred on Moray, dominated Pictland, and in the ninth century the Pictish kingdom merged with Dál Riata to form the Kingdom of Alba.

The Pictish language, an Insular Celtic language related to Brittonic, was gradually displaced by Gaelic from the late ninth century, and Pictish identity was forgotten, probably during the 11th century.
dyk: The Latin word Picti is most commonly explained as meaning 'painted', yet the nobles, hunters and warriors carved on Pictish stones are shown without obvious tattoos.
ev: The Latin name Picti first appears in a Roman panegyric
A monastery is founded at Portmahomack, in an area once assumed to be among the last converted
Bridei mac Beli defeats the Northumbrians at the Battle of Dun Nechtain, halting their northward expansion
Nechtan mac Der Ilei is reported to have expelled the monks and clergy of Iona
Óengus mac Fergusa reigns as Pictish king and holds Dál Riata subject
Vikings kill the King of Fortriu, Eógan mac Óengusa, and the King of Dál Riata in a major battle
Kenneth MacAlpin becomes king of the Picts
Under Caustantín mac Áeda outsiders begin to call the region the Kingdom of Alba

sections.origins:
The area the Picts occupied had earlier been described by Roman writers as the home of the Caledonii, alongside other tribes such as the Verturiones, Taexali and Venicones. The Picts are assumed to have been descendants of the Caledonii and other northern Iron Age tribes. The Latin word Picti first occurs in a panegyric of 297 and is most commonly explained as meaning 'painted', usually taken to refer to tattooing; an alternative suggestion links it to a native form, perhaps related to the Gallic Pictones. In Old Irish they were Cruithni and in Old Welsh Prydyn.

Bede's Ecclesiastical History of the English People tells of settlers from Scythia who landed in northern Ireland and were sent on to northern Britain, taking Scoti wives. This account has long been recognised as a pseudohistorical invention, probably of Pictish origin and composed around 700, meant to legitimise the annexation of Pictish territories by Fortriu. A 2023 study of eight whole genomes from Lundin Links in Fife and Balintore in Easter Ross found broad affinities with Iron Age Britons and present-day people of western Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland and Northumbria, supporting a local origin.

Scholars now stress that the Picts were a heterogeneous group. James Fraser argues the name was adopted as an endonym only in the late seventh century under the Verturian hegemony; Gordon Noble and Nicholas Evans think an earlier use plausible.
sections.society:
Like most northern European people in Late Antiquity, the Picts were farmers living in small communities. Cattle and horses were signs of wealth and prestige; sheep and pigs were kept in large numbers, and place names suggest that transhumance was common. They grew wheat, barley, oats and rye, with kale, cabbage, onions, leeks, peas, beans, turnips and skirret. Fish, shellfish, seals and whales were taken along coasts and rivers. Carvings show hunting with dogs and, unlike in Ireland, with falcons. Kilns dried grain in the changeable climate, and evidence of watermills has recently been found.

No towns are known in Scotland until the 12th century. Larger, but not large, settlements stood around royal forts such as Burghead or beside religious foundations. Most people lived in roundhouses and rectangular timbered halls; brochs, built earlier in the Iron Age, and crannogs stayed in use.

Pictland was made up of several kingdoms, with one king, sometimes two, dominating lesser neighbours; later sources speak of seven, among them Cait, Ce, Fib, Fotla and Fortriu, though the number may echo the seven sons of the mythical founder Cruithne. Succession often passed to brothers or cousins rather than sons, and the idea of matrilineal succession rests on Irish legends and a statement of Bede. Kingship became less personal and more institutional over time, and the later Mormaers are thought to have originated in Pictish times.
sections.beliefs:
Early Pictish religion is presumed to have resembled Celtic polytheism in general, although only place names remain from the pre-Christian era. When the Pictish elite converted to Christianity is uncertain. Traditions place Saint Palladius in Pictland and link Abernethy with Saint Brigid of Kildare; Saint Patrick refers to "apostate Picts"; and Bede wrote that Saint Ninian had converted the southern Picts. Excavation at Portmahomack places the foundation of its monastery in the late 6th century, in the time of Bridei mac Maelchon and Columba, but the spread of Christianity across Pictland took much longer.

Pictland had ties to Iona and Ireland and also to the churches of Northumbria. The reported expulsion of Ionan monks and clergy by Nechtan mac Der Ilei in 717 may have been linked to the dispute over the dating of Easter and the tonsure, where Nechtan seems to have supported Roman usage, or may have been meant to increase royal power over the church. Major religious sites of eastern Pictland included Portmahomack, Cennrígmonaid (later St Andrews), Dunkeld, Abernethy and Rosemarkie, which appear to be associated with Pictish kings.

The cult of saints mattered greatly. Kings venerated great saints, such as Saint Peter in the case of Nechtan, while lesser saints like Drostan had a wide following in the north, and noble kin groups appear to have had their own patron saints and churches.
sections.arts:
Pictish art is chiefly associated with monumental stones, but it also includes smaller objects of stone and bone and metalwork such as brooches. It developed a distinctive form of the Celtic La Tène style, with growing influence from the Insular art of 7th- and 8th-century Ireland and Northumbria. The symbols include animals such as the Pictish Beast, the "rectangle", the "mirror and comb", the "double-disc and Z-rod" and the "crescent and V-rod"; they have defied attempts at translation. Later cross-slabs combine these symbols with interlace and Christian images such as David the harpist and Daniel and the lion, drawn from the Insular manuscript tradition.

The Picts seem to have had a good deal of silver, probably from raiding further south or from subsidies paid to stop them. The largest hoard of early Pictish metalwork was found in 1819 at Norrie's Law in Fife, though much of it was dispersed and melted down; a 7th-century silver and enamel plaque from it shows a Z-rod. Over ten heavy silver chains, some over 0.5m long, survive, among them the Whitecleuch Chain, probably worn as a choker.

After Christianization, in the 8th and 9th centuries, the elite favoured penannular brooches with lobed terminals. The St Ninian's Isle Treasure (c. 750–825 AD) holds the best collection of Pictish forms, and the 8th-century Monymusk Reliquary mixes Pictish and Irish styles.
sections.exchange:
The early Picts are associated with piracy and raiding along the coasts of Roman Britain, and Pictish pirates were probably merchants on other occasions. Trade did not simply collapse with the Roman Empire: tableware and storage vessels from Gaul, probably carried up the Irish Sea, have been found, and this trade may have been controlled from Dunadd in Dál Riata. Missionaries, travelling clerics and exiles also moved between Pictland and its neighbours.

In the 7th century Northumbria was the most powerful kingdom in Britain, and the Picts were probably tributary to it until the reign of Bridei mac Beli, who defeated the Anglians at the Battle of Dun Nechtain in 685. Óengus mac Fergusa (reigned 729–761) held Dál Riata subject, and Caustantín mac Fergusa (793–820) placed his son Domnall on its throne, though Pictish attempts to dominate the Britons of Alt Clut (Strathclyde) failed.

The Viking Age brought great change. Vikings conquered and settled the islands and mainland areas such as Caithness and Sutherland, and in a major battle in 839 they killed the King of Fortriu, Eógan mac Óengusa, the King of Dál Riata, Áed mac Boanta, and many others. In the 840s Kenneth MacAlpin (Cináed mac Ailpín) became king of the Picts, and the Pictish kingdom merged with Dál Riata. Gaelic had long been advancing into Pictland: Atholl, meaning New Ireland, is attested in the early 8th century.
sections.legacy:
During the reign of Cínaed's grandson, Caustantín mac Áeda (900–943), outsiders began to call the region the Kingdom of Alba rather than the Kingdom of the Picts. It is not known whether a new kingdom had been established or Alba was simply closer to the Picts' own name for themselves. The Pictish language did not vanish at once, but Gaelicisation was clearly underway, and by a certain point, probably in the 11th century, the people of northern Alba had become fully Gaelicised Scots. Henry of Huntingdon noted the disappearance of the Picts in the mid-12th century.

The Pictish language is extinct, known only from place names, personal names, a few inscriptions and records in other languages. It is likely to have influenced the grammar and vocabulary of Scottish Gaelic, which has some features more reminiscent of the Brittonic languages. The ogham inscriptions on Pictish stones were argued by several linguists to be unintelligible as Celtic, and their nature is still debated.

The idea of the Picts as a tribe was later revived in myth and legend, and at the start of the twentieth century they were popularly seen as an exotic "lost people". The Problem of the Picts (1955) and later reappraisals of Bede and Adomnán have replaced that picture with one of a varied society much like its British, Gaelic and Anglo-Saxon neighbours, known today through the many Pictish stones and excavated sites such as Portmahomack.

summary: The Picts were the peoples of early medieval Scotland north of the Forth, first named by Romans in 297 and later united under the kingdom of Fortriu. Farmers, raiders and makers of carved symbol stones and fine silverwork, they merged with Dál Riata into the Kingdom of Alba and were fully Gaelicised, probably by the 11th century.
